title: Replication and consistency
summary: Say what a replica is for and what a client can see after a write.

body:
Rule. Replicas copy data for read scale, failover, or locality. Name the replication model: single-primary async, single-primary sync, or multi-primary. After a write, say whether a reader on a replica can see it immediately. Choose read-your-writes, bounded staleness, or strong reads explicitly for the user-visible path.

Why it matters. "We will add replicas" without a consistency sentence creates ghost reads — a user refreshes and loses their just-posted comment. Interviewers expect you to pick where strong reads matter and where lag is fine.

Worked example. Shortener primary takes writes. 3 read replicas serve GET redirects with async replication lag around 50 ms. A creator who shortens a URL and immediately tests the redirect may miss on a lagging replica — fix by reading the primary for the creator session, or by warming cache on write. Social likes can tolerate short lag; bank ledger transfers cannot. Failover: if the primary dies, promote a replica only after acknowledging possible loss of the last unreplicated writes under async replication, or use sync replication to a standby at the cost of write latency. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool.

When to use. Add replicas when read QPS or availability needs exceed one node. State the consistency choice next to each user-visible read. Use primary reads for read-your-writes sessions when lag would confuse users.

When to refuse. Refuse promising zero data loss with async replication. Refuse sending every read to the primary after adding replicas "for scale." Refuse multi-primary conflict resolution stories you cannot finish in the hour. Refuse ignoring failover for the write path.
